title: Can an angle tell how much an insect has turned?
description: An insect is drawn in one position and again after it has turned. A horizontal line touches both. The two arms of the angle and its vertex are found, to see that an angle can describe the amount of rotation.
teaching_notes: One idea: the amount of rotation is an angle, with the horizontal line as one arm, the line along the turned insect as the other arm, and the vertex where the turn happens. Watch for students who look for a drawn angle and say there is none.

source: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q5
video_script.why: The child finds the two arms and the vertex of an angle that is not drawn, here in a turned picture, as the solved example did for the clock hands.
video_script.substitution: The insect and its rotated copy of the book's question.
video_script.anchor: the insect of the book, drawn once on a horizontal line and again after it has turned about a point on that line
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, an angle can describe the amount of rotation

final_answer.value: Yes; the horizontal line is one arm and the line along the rotated insect is the other arm; the vertex is the point of rotation on the line
final_answer.spoken: the horizontal line is one arm and the line along the rotated insect is the other arm

maths_rules: an angle has two arms that meet at a vertex
the horizontal line touching the insect is one arm
the line along the rotated insect is the other arm
the vertex is the point of rotation on the horizontal line, which does not move when the insect turns
video_script.design: The insect and its turned copy stay on the board. The two arms light up one at a time, then the place that does not move is found, and the words point of rotation are held back until the answer line.
open_questions: The book answer is open-ended and the figure is not in the extracted text. The video follows the worklist: the horizontal line is one arm, the line along the rotated insect is the other, and the vertex is the point of rotation.
